blocks.body:
Euclid's argument shows that there are infinitely many primes, and small variations of it show that there are infinitely many primes of the form $4k+3$, or of the form $4k+1$. Arguments of that polynomial type are known to work only for special progressions, so they cannot answer the general question: if $\gcd(a,q)=1$, does the progression $a, a+q, a+2q, \dots$ contain infinitely many primes?

Dirichlet answered it in 1837. To each character $\chi$ modulo $q$ he attached a function $L(s,\chi)$, and he showed that the whole problem comes down to one fact: $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$ for every non-principal character $\chi$. This lesson builds these functions, explains why that fact is exactly what is needed, and proves it.

blocks.title: From Euler's proof to characters
blocks.body:
Start with Euler's proof that $\sum_p 1/p$ diverges, in the language of [[zeta]]. For real $s>1$ the Euler product gives
$$\log \zeta(s) = \sum_p -\log(1-p^{-s}) = \sum_p \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{1}{k p^{ks}}.$$
The terms with $k \ge 2$ add up to less than $\sum_p \sum_{k\ge 2} p^{-k} = \sum_p \frac{1}{p(p-1)} < 1$. Also $\zeta(s) = \frac{1}{s-1} + O(1)$ as $s \to 1^+$. Together,
$$\sum_p p^{-s} = \log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1) \qquad (s \to 1^+),$$
which could not tend to infinity if there were only finitely many primes.

To run the same argument on a single residue class we need a way to pick out the integers $n \equiv a \pmod q$. Characters do this. By the orthogonality relations from [[dirichlet-characters]], if $\gcd(a,q)=1$ then
$$\frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\chi \bmod q} \overline{\chi}(a)\,\chi(n) = \begin{cases} 1 & n \equiv a \pmod q,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
Multiplying by $p^{-s}$ and summing over primes,
$$\sum_{p \equiv a \ (q)} p^{-s} = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\chi} \overline{\chi}(a) \sum_p \chi(p)\, p^{-s}.$$
The principal character $\chi_0$ contributes $\sum_{p \nmid q} p^{-s} = \log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1)$. So the theorem will follow once we know that, for every $\chi \ne \chi_0$, the sum $\sum_p \chi(p)p^{-s}$ stays bounded as $s \to 1^+$. That is a statement about $L(s,\chi)$.

blocks.title: Dirichlet L-function
blocks.body:
For a Dirichlet character $\chi$ modulo $q$ and $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
$$L(s,\chi) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\chi(n)}{n^s} = \prod_p \Bigl(1 - \frac{\chi(p)}{p^s}\Bigr)^{-1}.$$
The series converges absolutely because $|\chi(n)| \le 1$, and the product formula holds because $\chi$ is completely multiplicative (see [[dirichlet-series]]). The Euler product is what ties $L(s,\chi)$ to the values $\chi(p)$.

blocks.title: Three basic facts
blocks.body:
1. The principal character. Since $\chi_0(n)=1$ exactly when $\gcd(n,q)=1$, the Euler product gives $L(s,\chi_0) = \zeta(s)\prod_{p \mid q}(1-p^{-s})$. So $L(s,\chi_0)$ has a simple pole at $s=1$, just like $\zeta(s)$.

2. Non-principal characters converge further left. Let $A(x) = \sum_{n \le x}\chi(n)$. For $\chi \ne \chi_0$ the values of $\chi$ over any $q$ consecutive integers add up to $0$, and an incomplete block contains at most $\varphi(q)$ non-zero values, so $|A(x)| \le \varphi(q)$ for all $x$. By [[partial-summation]], if $f$ is positive and decreasing on $[t,u]$ then
$$\Bigl|\sum_{t < n \le u} \chi(n) f(n)\Bigr| = \Bigl|A(u)f(u) - A(t)f(t) - \int_t^u A(v) f'(v)\,dv\Bigr| \le 2\varphi(q) f(t).$$
With $f(n) = n^{-s}$ this shows that $\sum \chi(n)n^{-s}$ converges for every real $s>0$, with tails $|\sum_{n>t}\chi(n)n^{-s}| \le 2\varphi(q)t^{-s}$. In particular $L(1,\chi) = \sum_{n \ge 1}\chi(n)/n$ converges (not absolutely). The same argument applied to $\sum \chi(n)(\log n) n^{-s}$ shows that $L(s,\chi)$ is continuously differentiable for $s>0$.

3. A logarithm with a known main term. For $s>1$ put
$$\ell(s,\chi) = \sum_p \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{\chi(p)^k}{k\,p^{ks}}.$$
Using $-\log(1-z) = \sum_k z^k/k$ for $|z|<1$ in each Euler factor, $e^{\ell(s,\chi)} = L(s,\chi)$; in particular $L(s,\chi) \ne 0$ for $s>1$. As in Euler's computation, the terms with $k\ge 2$ contribute less than $1$ in absolute value, so
$$\ell(s,\chi) = \sum_p \chi(p)p^{-s} + O(1) \quad\text{uniformly for } s>1.$$

blocks.title: Dirichlet's theorem (conditional form)
blocks.body:
Let $q \ge 1$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$. If $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$ for every non-principal character $\chi$ modulo $q$, then
$$\sum_{p \equiv a \ (q)} \frac{1}{p^s} = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)}\log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1) \qquad (s \to 1^+).$$
In particular, there are infinitely many primes $p \equiv a \pmod q$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Fix $\chi \ne \chi_0$. By fact 2, $L(s,\chi)$ is continuous on $[1,2]$; it is non-zero on $(1,2]$ by fact 3 and at $s=1$ by hypothesis. A continuous non-vanishing function on an interval has a continuous logarithm $\lambda(s)$ there, and $\lambda$ is bounded because $[1,2]$ is compact. On $(1,2]$ both $\lambda$ and $\ell(\cdot,\chi)$ are continuous logarithms of $L(\cdot,\chi)$, so their difference is a continuous function with values in $2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$, hence constant. Therefore $\ell(s,\chi)$ is bounded on $(1,2]$, and by fact 3 so is $\sum_p \chi(p)p^{-s}$.

For $\chi_0$ we have $$\sum_p \chi_0(p)p^{-s} = \sum_p p^{-s} - \sum_{p \mid q}p^{-s} = \log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1)$$ by Euler's computation. Inserting both facts into the orthogonality formula of the first section gives the stated asymptotic. If there were only finitely many primes $p \equiv a \pmod q$, the left side would stay bounded as $s \to 1^+$, while the right side tends to infinity.

blocks.title: The finer statement
blocks.body:
With Mertens-type estimates in place of the limit $s \to 1^+$, the same strategy gives the key statement: for $\gcd(a,q)=1$,
$$\sum_{\substack{p \le x \\ p \equiv a \ (q)}} \frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \log\log x + O(1),$$
where the $O(1)$ depends on $q$. Compared with $\sum_{p \le x} 1/p = \log\log x + O(1)$ from [[mertens]], each of the $\varphi(q)$ admissible classes receives an equal share. The extra input is that $\sum_{p \le x}\chi(p)/p$ stays bounded for $\chi \ne \chi_0$, again a consequence of $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$; we omit it (Apostol, Chapter 7, proves the version with weights $\log p/p$).

The stronger statement that each class contains asymptotically $\pi(x)/\varphi(q)$ primes up to $x$ is the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions (de la Vallée Poussin, 1896). It needs $L(s,\chi) \ne 0$ on the whole line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$; see [[pnt]] and [[zero-free-region]].

blocks.title: Why L(1, χ) is not zero: complex characters
blocks.body:
Everything now rests on $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$. The first step is a positivity property of the product of all the $L$-functions modulo $q$.

Lemma. For real $s>1$, $\prod_{\chi \bmod q} L(s,\chi)$ is real and at least $1$.

Proof. Summing the series for $\ell(s,\chi)$ over all $\chi$ and using orthogonality,
$$\sum_{\chi}\ell(s,\chi) = \sum_p\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{1}{k p^{ks}}\sum_\chi \chi(p^k) = \varphi(q)\sum_{p^k \equiv 1 \ (q)} \frac{1}{k p^{ks}} \ \ge\ 0.$$
Exponentiating gives $\prod_\chi L(s,\chi) = e^{\sum_\chi \ell(s,\chi)} \ge 1$.

Now suppose $\chi \ne \overline{\chi}$ (a complex character) and $L(1,\chi)=0$. Then also $L(1,\overline\chi) = \overline{L(1,\chi)} = 0$. As $s \to 1^+$: the factor $L(s,\chi_0)$ is at most $C/(s-1)$; the two factors $L(s,\chi)$ and $L(s,\overline\chi)$ are each at most $C(s-1)$ in absolute value, because they are differentiable at $1$ and vanish there; every other factor is bounded. So the product is $O(s-1)$ and tends to $0$, contradicting the lemma. Hence $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$ for every complex character.

For a real character $\chi = \overline\chi$ this argument gives nothing: a single zero at $s=1$ would exactly cancel the simple pole of $L(s,\chi_0)$, and the product could still be at least $1$. Real characters need their own argument.

blocks.title: Non-vanishing for real characters
blocks.body: If $\chi$ is a real non-principal character modulo $q$, then $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $r(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\chi(d)$. This is multiplicative, and on prime powers $r(p^k) = 1 + \chi(p) + \dots + \chi(p)^k$ equals $k+1$, $1$, or ($1$ if $k$ is even, $0$ if $k$ is odd) according as $\chi(p) = 1, 0, -1$. Hence $r(n) \ge 0$ for all $n$, and $r(n) \ge 1$ when $n$ is a perfect square.

Consider $G(x) = \sum_{n \le x} r(n)/\sqrt n$. Keeping only the squares $n = m^2$,
$$G(x) \ \ge\ \sum_{m \le \sqrt x}\frac{1}{m} \ \ge\ \log\sqrt x = \tfrac12\log x.$$
On the other hand $G(x) = \sum_{dm \le x}\chi(d)/\sqrt{dm}$. Put $y = \sqrt x$ and split the pairs $(d,m)$ with $dm \le x$ into those with $d \le y$ and those with $d > y$ (which forces $m < y$):
$$G(x) = \sum_{d \le y}\frac{\chi(d)}{\sqrt d}\sum_{m \le x/d}\frac{1}{\sqrt m} \;+\; \sum_{m \le y}\frac{1}{\sqrt m}\sum_{y < d \le x/m}\frac{\chi(d)}{\sqrt d}.$$
We use two estimates, with constants depending only on $q$: comparison with an integral gives $\sum_{m \le t} m^{-1/2} = 2\sqrt t + c_0 + O(t^{-1/2})$ for $t \ge 1$ and some constant $c_0$; and fact 2 gives $|\sum_{t<d\le u}\chi(d)d^{-1/2}| \le 2\varphi(q)t^{-1/2}$ and $\sum_{d \le y}\chi(d)/d = L(1,\chi) + O(1/y)$.

In the first double sum, the inner sum is $2\sqrt{x/d} + c_0 + O(\sqrt{d/x})$, so the first part equals
$$2\sqrt x\sum_{d\le y}\frac{\chi(d)}{d} + c_0\sum_{d\le y}\frac{\chi(d)}{\sqrt d} + O\Bigl(\frac{y}{\sqrt x}\Bigr) = 2\sqrt x\,L(1,\chi) + O(1),$$
because $\sqrt x \cdot O(1/y) = O(1)$, the partial sums of the convergent series $\sum \chi(d)/\sqrt d$ are bounded, and $y/\sqrt x = 1$. In the second part each inner sum is $O(y^{-1/2})$ and $\sum_{m \le y} m^{-1/2} \le 2\sqrt y$, so it is $O(1)$. Therefore
$$G(x) = 2\sqrt x\,L(1,\chi) + O(1).$$
If $L(1,\chi)$ were $0$, $G(x)$ would be bounded, contradicting $G(x) \ge \frac12\log x$.

blocks.title: The two classes modulo 4
blocks.body: Let $\chi_4$ be the non-principal character modulo $4$ ($\chi_4(n) = 1, -1, 0$ for $n \equiv 1, 3$, even). Compute $L(1,\chi_4)$, explain how the proof separates the primes $p \equiv 1$ from $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and compare the sums $\sum 1/p$ over the two classes for $p \le 10^6$.
blocks.solution:
Here $L(1,\chi_4) = 1 - \frac13 + \frac15 - \frac17 + \dots = \frac{\pi}{4}$ (Leibniz's series, the value of $\arctan 1$). The two indicator functions are $\frac12(\chi_0 + \chi_4)$ for the class $1$ and $\frac12(\chi_0 - \chi_4)$ for the class $3$, so
$$\sum_{p \equiv 1\,(4)} p^{-s} = \tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_{p>2}p^{-s} + \sum_p\chi_4(p)p^{-s}\Bigr),\qquad \sum_{p \equiv 3\,(4)} p^{-s} = \tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_{p>2}p^{-s} - \sum_p\chi_4(p)p^{-s}\Bigr).$$
The first sum in each bracket is $\log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1)$, and the second stays bounded because $L(1,\chi_4) = \pi/4 \ne 0$. So both classes get half of the divergence.

Numerically, for $p \le 10^6$ one finds $\sum_{p\equiv 1\,(4)} 1/p \approx 1.026$ and $\sum_{p \equiv 3\,(4)}1/p \approx 1.361$, while $\frac12\log\log 10^6 \approx 1.313$. Both sums grow like $\frac12\log\log x$; their difference is a bounded quantity (the prime $3$ alone contributes $1/3$ to it).

blocks.title: Lattice points and the value π/4
blocks.body: For $\chi = \chi_4$ the function $r(n) = \sum_{d\mid n}\chi_4(d)$ from the proof has a geometric meaning: the number of pairs $(u,v)\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ with $u^2+v^2 = n$ equals $4r(n)$ for $n \ge 1$ (Jacobi's two-square formula, see [[sums-of-squares]]). Use this to show again that $L(1,\chi_4) = \pi/4$.
blocks.solution:
Summing over $n \le x$, the left side counts lattice points $(u,v) \ne (0,0)$ in the disc $u^2+v^2 \le x$, which is $\pi x + O(\sqrt x)$ (compare each lattice point with the unit square it is the corner of). So $\sum_{n\le x}r(n) = \frac{\pi}{4}x + O(\sqrt x)$.

On the other hand $\sum_{n \le x}r(n) = \sum_{dm \le x}\chi_4(d)$. Splitting at $y = \sqrt x$ as in the proof (Dirichlet's hyperbola method),
$$\sum_{dm\le x}\chi_4(d) = \sum_{d\le y}\chi_4(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\Bigr\rfloor + \sum_{m \le y}A\Bigl(\frac{x}{m}\Bigr) - A(y)\lfloor y\rfloor,$$
with $A(t) = \sum_{n\le t}\chi_4(n) \in \{0,1\}$. The first sum is $x\sum_{d \le y}\chi_4(d)/d + O(y) = x\,L(1,\chi_4) + O(\sqrt x)$, and the other two terms are $O(\sqrt x)$. Comparing, $x\,L(1,\chi_4) = \frac{\pi}{4}x + O(\sqrt x)$; divide by $x$ and let $x \to \infty$.

For $x = 10^6$ the disc contains $3\,141\,549$ lattice points, so $\sum_{n \le 10^6} r(n) = 785\,387$, against $\frac{\pi}{4}\cdot 10^6 \approx 785\,398$. The sum $G(x)$ of the proof behaves as predicted too: at $x = 10^6$, $G(x) - 2\sqrt x\cdot\frac{\pi}{4} \approx -0.99$.

blocks.title: Two progressions without L-functions
blocks.body: Prove, with elementary arguments only, that there are infinitely many primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and infinitely many primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
blocks.solution:
Class $3$. Given any finite list $p_1,\dots,p_k$ of primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, let $N = 4p_1\cdots p_k - 1$. Then $N$ is odd and $N \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. A product of integers that are all $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ is $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, so $N$ has a prime factor $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. It is not any $p_i$, since $N \equiv -1 \pmod{p_i}$.

Class $1$. Given any finite list $p_1,\dots,p_k$ of primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, let $M = (2p_1\cdots p_k)^2 + 1$ and let $p$ be a prime factor of $M$. Then $p$ is odd, $p \ne p_i$, and $(2p_1\cdots p_k)^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p$, so $-1$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$. By [[quadratic-residues]] this forces $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

Both proofs use a polynomial whose prime divisors are confined to the desired classes; as the introduction says, this trick does not extend to general progressions.

blocks.body:
- The Euler product does not converge absolutely at $s=1$, and its convergence there is not evident (it is in fact a deep fact, of the strength of the prime number theorem for progressions). So $L(1,\chi)$ is defined as the sum of the conditionally convergent series $\sum \chi(n)/n$, equivalently the limit of $L(s,\chi)$ as $s \to 1^+$, not by putting $s=1$ into the product.
- The condition $\gcd(a,q)=1$ is essential: if $\gcd(a,q) = d > 1$, every term of the progression is divisible by $d$, so it contains at most one prime.
- If $\chi$ is induced by a primitive character $\chi^*$, then $L(s,\chi) = L(s,\chi^*)\prod_{p\mid q}(1-\chi^*(p)p^{-s})$. The extra factors do not vanish at $s=1$, so non-vanishing at $1$ can be checked on primitive characters.

For real characters Dirichlet went further and computed $L(1,\chi)$ exactly in terms of class numbers of quadratic forms: see [[class-number-formula]]. How small $L(1,\chi)$ can be, and how close to $1$ a real zero of $L(s,\chi)$ can lie, is the subject of [[siegel-zeros]] and [[no-siegel]]; the generalized Riemann hypothesis [[grh]] asserts that all non-trivial zeros lie on $\operatorname{Re} s = \frac12$. The zeros control the error term for primes in progressions through the [[explicit-formula]], and averages of $|L(\frac12 + it,\chi)|^2$ are the subject of [[moments]].

The template generalizes: [[hecke-l]] attaches $L$-functions to characters of ideal class groups of number fields, and the conjecture of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer [[bsd]] predicts the behaviour at $s=1$ of the $L$-function of an elliptic curve.

1. Using the primitive root $2$ modulo $5$, list the four characters modulo $5$ and write the indicator function of the class $n \equiv 2 \pmod 5$ as a combination of them.
2. Prove that $|\sum_{n\le x}\chi(n)| \le \varphi(q)$ for every non-principal $\chi$ modulo $q$, and deduce that $\sum_n \chi(n)/n$ converges.
3. For the real character $\chi$ modulo $3$, compute $r(n) = \sum_{d\mid n}\chi(d)$ for $1 \le n \le 12$ and check that $r(n) \ge 0$, with $r(n) \ge 1$ at the squares.

blocks.body:
For a real character $\chi$, the proof that $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$ in [[l-functions]] is a clever estimate. Dirichlet's own route was different and much more informative: in 1839 he computed $L(1,\chi)$ exactly when $\chi$ is the character attached to a quadratic discriminant $D$. The answer is a simple multiple of the number $h(D)$ of classes of binary quadratic forms of discriminant $D$. Since a class number is at least $1$, positivity of $L(1,\chi)$ comes for free.

The formula works in both directions. It turns analytic questions about the size of $L(1,\chi_D)$ into arithmetic questions about class numbers, and arithmetic facts into analytic ones. This is why the problem of Siegel zeros and Gauss's class number problem are two faces of the same question.

blocks.title: The two sides of the formula
blocks.body:
Let $D<0$ be a discriminant, that is $D \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$. As in [[quadratic-forms]], consider forms $f(x,y) = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$ with $b^2 - 4ac = D$ that are positive definite ($a>0$) and primitive ($\gcd(a,b,c) = 1$). The group $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ acts on them by invertible integral changes of variables, and $h(D)$ is the number of orbits (classes). Each class contains exactly one reduced form, meaning $|b| \le a \le c$, with $b \ge 0$ whenever $|b| = a$ or $a = c$; so $h(D)$ can be computed by a finite search.

Write $w = w(D)$ for the number of elements of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ that fix a given form: $w = 6$ for $D=-3$, $w=4$ for $D=-4$, and $w=2$ for all other $D<0$.

On the analytic side, $\chi_D(n) = \bigl(\frac{D}{n}\bigr)$ is the Kronecker symbol. It is a real non-principal character modulo $|D|$. For example $\chi_{-4}$ is the character $\chi_4$ modulo $4$, $\chi_{-3}(n) = \bigl(\frac{n}{3}\bigr)$, and for a prime $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, $\chi_{-p}(n) = \bigl(\frac{n}{p}\bigr)$ by quadratic reciprocity. At $n = 2$ the Kronecker symbol is $0$ for even $D$, $+1$ for $D \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ and $-1$ for $D \equiv 5 \pmod 8$.

blocks.title: Class number h(D)
blocks.body: For a discriminant $D<0$, $h(D)$ is the number of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$-equivalence classes of primitive positive definite binary quadratic forms of discriminant $D$. It measures how far representation of integers by forms of discriminant $D$ is from being decided by a single form.

blocks.title: Dirichlet's class number formula (D < 0)
blocks.body:
For every discriminant $D<0$,
$$L(1, \chi_D) = \frac{2\pi\, h(D)}{w \sqrt{|D|}}.$$
In particular $L(1,\chi_D) = \pi h(D)/\sqrt{|D|}$ for $D<-4$.

blocks.title: Proof for fundamental discriminants
blocks.body:
We give the proof when $D$ is fundamental (not of the form $f^2D'$ with $f>1$ and $D'$ a smaller discriminant); the general case follows the same pattern, with Step 1 replaced by the corresponding count for non-fundamental discriminants (or it can be deduced from the fundamental case using the known relation between $h(f^2D)$ and $h(D)$). The proof counts lattice points in two ways. For a form $f$ let $r_f(n)$ be the number of $(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ with $f(x,y) = n$, and choose one form $f_1, \dots, f_h$ from each class.

Step 1 (representation count; proof omitted). For fundamental $D<0$ and every $n \ge 1$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{h} r_{f_i}(n) = w\sum_{d\mid n}\chi_D(d).$$
This is Dirichlet's formula for the total number of representations by a full set of classes. In the language of [[ideals]] it says that each ideal of norm $n$ in the imaginary quadratic field of discriminant $D$ is counted $w$ times. For $D=-4$ it is Jacobi's formula for sums of two squares.

Step 2 (geometry). For a single form, $\sum_{n \le X} r_f(n)$ counts the lattice points $(x,y) \ne (0,0)$ in the ellipse $f(x,y) \le X$. Completing the square, $f(x,y) = a\bigl(x + \frac{b}{2a}y\bigr)^2 + \frac{|D|}{4a}y^2$; the linear substitution $u = \sqrt a\,(x + \frac{b}{2a}y)$, $v = \sqrt{|D|/(4a)}\,y$ has determinant $\sqrt{|D|}/2$ and maps the ellipse onto the disc $u^2+v^2 \le X$. So the ellipse has area $\pi X/(\sqrt{|D|}/2) = 2\pi X/\sqrt{|D|}$. The number of lattice points in a convex region dilated by $\sqrt X$ is its area plus $O(\sqrt X)$, hence
$$\sum_{n\le X}\sum_{i} r_{f_i}(n) = \frac{2\pi h}{\sqrt{|D|}}X + O(\sqrt X).$$

Step 3 (analysis). By Dirichlet's hyperbola method, exactly as in the lattice-point example of [[l-functions]],
$$\sum_{n \le X}\sum_{d \mid n}\chi_D(d) = X\,L(1,\chi_D) + O(\sqrt X).$$

Combining the three steps, $\frac{2\pi h}{\sqrt{|D|}}X + O(\sqrt X) = wX\,L(1,\chi_D) + O(\sqrt X)$. Dividing by $X$ and letting $X \to \infty$ gives the formula.

blocks.title: Finite formulas and a curious consequence
blocks.body:
$L(1,\chi)$ is an infinite series, but for these characters it can be summed in closed form using [[gauss-sums]]. For an odd primitive character $\chi$ modulo $q$ one has
$$L(1,\chi) = \frac{\pi i\,\tau(\chi)}{q^2}\sum_{a=1}^{q}\overline\chi(a)\,a,$$
where $\tau(\chi)$ is the Gauss sum. Take $q = p$ a prime with $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, $p>3$, and $\chi(n) = \bigl(\frac{n}{p}\bigr)$. Then $\tau(\chi) = i\sqrt p$, and the class number formula becomes
$$h(-p) = -\frac{1}{p}\sum_{a=1}^{p-1} a\Bigl(\frac{a}{p}\Bigr).$$
A further rearrangement gives
$$\Bigl(2 - \Bigl(\frac{2}{p}\Bigr)\Bigr)\,h(-p) = \sum_{a=1}^{(p-1)/2}\Bigl(\frac{a}{p}\Bigr).$$
We omit these derivations (see Davenport, Chapter 6). The second formula has a striking consequence. Since $h(-p) \ge 1$, for every prime $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ there are more quadratic residues than non-residues in the interval $1 \le a \le (p-1)/2$. The statement is entirely elementary, but the standard proof goes through $L(1,\chi)$.

blocks.title: Positive discriminants
blocks.body:
For a fundamental discriminant $D>0$ the corresponding formula, stated here without proof, is
$$L(1,\chi_D) = \frac{2\,h(D)\log\varepsilon_D}{\sqrt D},$$
where now $h(D)$ is the class number of the real quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt D)$ and $\varepsilon_D > 1$ is its fundamental unit. For $D = 5$: $h = 1$, $\varepsilon = \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$, and $L(1,\chi_5) = 2\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}/\sqrt5 \approx 0.4304$.

The regulator $\log\varepsilon_D$ can be large (the formula, with $h \ge 1$ and $L(1,\chi_D) \ll \log D$, only bounds it by $O(\sqrt D\log D)$), and when it is large a normal-sized $L(1,\chi_D)$ is compatible with a very small class number. That is why class numbers of real quadratic fields behave so differently: Gauss's conjecture that infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number $1$ is still open.

blocks.title: What the formula is used for
blocks.body:
1. An effective lower bound. Since $h(D) \ge 1$, $L(1,\chi_D) \ge \pi/\sqrt{|D|}$ for $D<-4$. This is weak but completely explicit.

2. An upper bound for class numbers. Splitting $\sum\chi(n)/n$ at $n = q$ and using the tail bound $2\varphi(q)/q \le 2$ from [[l-functions]] gives $L(1,\chi) \le \log q + 3$ for any non-principal $\chi$ modulo $q$. Hence $h(D) \le \frac{\sqrt{|D|}}{\pi}(\log|D| + 3)$ for $D < -4$.

3. Gauss's class number problem. Gauss conjectured that $h(D) \to \infty$ as $D \to -\infty$; Heilbronn proved it in 1934. The fundamental discriminants $D<0$ with $h(D)=1$ are exactly
$$-3,\ -4,\ -7,\ -8,\ -11,\ -19,\ -43,\ -67,\ -163,$$
a list completed by Heegner (1952), Baker (1966) and Stark (1967).

4. Siegel zeros. By the formula, a lower bound for $L(1,\chi_D)$ is the same thing as a lower bound for $h(D)$. Siegel's theorem $L(1,\chi_D) \gg_\varepsilon |D|^{-\varepsilon}$ is equivalent to $h(D) \gg_\varepsilon |D|^{1/2-\varepsilon}$, and a real zero of $L(s,\chi_D)$ very close to $1$ would force $h(D)$ to be unusually small. See [[siegel-zeros]].

blocks.title: The two smallest discriminants
blocks.body: Check the formula for $D = -4$ and $D = -3$.
blocks.solution:
For $D=-4$ the only reduced form is $x^2+y^2$, so $h = 1$, and $w = 4$ (the rotations $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)$ and its powers fix it). The formula predicts $L(1,\chi_{-4}) = 2\pi/(4\cdot 2) = \pi/4$, which is Leibniz's series $1 - \frac13 + \frac15 - \dots$.

For $D=-3$ the only reduced form is $x^2+xy+y^2$, $h=1$, $w=6$. The formula predicts $L(1,\chi_{-3}) = 2\pi/(6\sqrt3) = \pi/(3\sqrt3) \approx 0.6046$, which agrees with $1 - \frac12 + \frac14 - \frac15 + \frac17 - \dots$.

blocks.title: Discriminant −23
blocks.body: Find $h(-23)$, check Step 1 of the proof for $n = 2$, and evaluate $L(1,\chi_{-23})$.
blocks.solution:
Reduced forms need $3a^2 \le |D| = 23$, so $a \le 2$, and $b \equiv D \pmod 2$, so $b$ is odd. For $a=1$: $b = 1$, $c = 6$. For $a = 2$: $b = \pm1$, $c = 3$. So the reduced forms are $x^2+xy+6y^2$, $2x^2+xy+3y^2$, $2x^2-xy+3y^2$, and $h(-23) = 3$.

For $n=2$: the first form never takes the value $2$ (it is at least $\frac{23}{4}y^2$ when $y \ne 0$, and $x^2$ when $y=0$), and each of the other two takes it exactly at $(\pm1, 0)$. Total: $4$ representations. On the other side, $-23 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ gives $\chi_{-23}(2) = 1$, so $w(\chi_{-23}(1) + \chi_{-23}(2)) = 2\cdot 2 = 4$.

The formula gives $L(1,\chi_{-23}) = 2\pi\cdot 3/(2\sqrt{23}) = 3\pi/\sqrt{23} \approx 1.9652$, which matches a direct numerical evaluation of the series.

blocks.title: Counting residues in the first half
blocks.body: For $p = 7, 11, 19, 23$, count the quadratic residues and non-residues among $1, 2, \dots, \frac{p-1}{2}$ and compare with $h(-p)$.
blocks.solution:
Write $S = \sum_{a \le (p-1)/2}\bigl(\frac{a}{p}\bigr)$, the number of residues minus the number of non-residues in the first half.

- $p=7$: residues $1,2,4$. In $\{1,2,3\}$: $1, 2$ are residues, $3$ is not, so $S = 1$. Here $\bigl(\frac27\bigr) = 1$, so $h(-7) = S/(2-1) = 1$.
- $p=11$: residues $1,3,4,5,9$. In $\{1,\dots,5\}$ only $2$ is a non-residue, so $S = 3$. Here $\bigl(\frac{2}{11}\bigr) = -1$, so $h(-11) = 3/3 = 1$.
- $p=19$: residues $1,4,5,6,7,9,11,16,17$. In $\{1,\dots,9\}$ the non-residues are $2,3,8$, so $S = 6-3 = 3$. Here $\bigl(\frac{2}{19}\bigr) = -1$, so $h(-19) = 1$.
- $p = 23$: residues $1,2,3,4,6,8,9,12,13,16,18$. In $\{1,\dots,11\}$ there are $7$ residues and $4$ non-residues, $S = 3$, and $\bigl(\frac{2}{23}\bigr)=1$, so $h(-23) = 3$, as found above.

In every case $S>0$, as the class number formula guarantees.

blocks.body:
- Forget $w$ and the formula is off by a factor of $2$ or $3$ for $D=-4$ and $D=-3$.
- $h(D)$ counts classes under $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ (proper equivalence). Under $GL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ the forms $2x^2 \pm xy + 3y^2$ become equivalent and one would count $2$ instead of $3$ for $D=-23$.
- $\chi_D$ is the Kronecker symbol $\bigl(\frac{D}{n}\bigr)$, including its value at $2$. For odd $D$ (so $D \equiv 1 \pmod 4$) it agrees with the Jacobi symbol $\bigl(\frac{n}{|D|}\bigr)$, but for even $D$ the Jacobi symbol modulo $|D|$ is not even defined.
- The formula is not restricted to fundamental discriminants, provided $h(D)$ counts primitive forms and $\chi_D$ is the Kronecker symbol. For $D = -12$: $h = 1$ (the form $2x^2+2xy+2y^2$ is not primitive), $w = 2$, and $L(1,\chi_{-12}) = \pi/(2\sqrt3)$.
- For $D > 0$ the regulator $\log\varepsilon_D$ appears, so the formula alone does not say that small $L(1,\chi_D)$ means small class number.

The formula is the case of an imaginary quadratic field of the analytic class number formula for the Dedekind zeta function: $\zeta_K(s) = \zeta(s)L(s,\chi_D)$, and the residue of $\zeta_K$ at $s=1$ is expressed through the class number of $K$ (see [[dedekind-zeta]] and [[class-group]]). The cases $D=-4$ and $D=-3$ are the arithmetic of [[gaussian-integers]] and [[eisenstein-integers]].

Its most important use in analytic number theory is the link between small values of $L(1,\chi_D)$, real zeros near $s = 1$, and small class numbers: [[siegel-zeros]]. The conjecture of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer [[bsd]] has the same shape, an $L$-value at $s=1$ expressed through arithmetic invariants.

2. Prove that $L(1,\chi) \le \log q + 3$ for every non-principal character $\chi$ modulo $q$, and deduce $h(D) \le \frac{\sqrt{|D|}}{\pi}(\log|D|+3)$ for $D<-4$.

4. Explain why, for $D<0$, the statements $L(1,\chi_D) \gg_\varepsilon |D|^{-\varepsilon}$ and $h(D) \gg_\varepsilon |D|^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ are equivalent.

blocks.body:
Dirichlet proved that $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$. Every quantitative use of $L$-functions needs more: how small can $L(1,\chi)$ be, and how close to $s=1$ can a zero of $L(s,\chi)$ lie? For complex characters, and for zeros off the real axis, the classical zero-free region gives a satisfactory answer. One possibility has resisted all attempts at exclusion: a real character $\chi$ modulo $q$ whose $L$-function has a real zero $\beta$ extremely close to $1$. Such a hypothetical zero is called a Siegel zero (also an exceptional or Landau–Siegel zero).

Nobody expects Siegel zeros to exist; the generalized Riemann hypothesis would rule them out completely. But the question of excluding them unconditionally has for decades been one of the central open problems of analytic number theory, and the best unconditional result, Siegel's theorem of 1935, comes with a constant that no one knows how to compute.

blocks.title: Where the exceptional zero comes from
blocks.body:
The zero-free region for Dirichlet $L$-functions (see [[zero-free-region]]) has a gap in it. The standard statement, due to Landau and Page, reads as follows; we do not prove it here.

There is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for every $q$, the product $\prod_{\chi \bmod q}L(s,\chi)$ has at most one zero $s = \sigma + it$ in the region
$$\sigma > 1 - \frac{c}{\log\bigl(q(|t|+2)\bigr)}.$$
If this zero exists, it is real and simple, and it is a zero of $L(s,\chi_1)$ for a real non-principal character $\chi_1$.

The proof of the zero-free region uses the inequality $3 + 4\cos\theta + \cos2\theta \ge 0$ applied to $L(s,\chi_0)^3L(s+it,\chi)^4L(s+2it,\chi^2)$. When $\chi$ is real and $t$ is close to $0$, the character $\chi^2$ is principal and $L(s+2it,\chi^2)$ has a pole near $s=1$ instead of being harmless, and the argument breaks down. That single gap is the exceptional zero.

blocks.title: Siegel zero
blocks.body:
Let $\chi$ be a real primitive character modulo $q$ and $\beta$ a real zero of $L(s,\chi)$. Informally, $\beta$ is a Siegel zero if $1-\beta$ is small compared with $1/\log q$. Precisely, Siegel zeros exist if there is a sequence of real primitive characters $\chi_j$ modulo $q_j$ with real zeros $\beta_j$ such that
$$(1-\beta_j)\log q_j \to 0.$$
The Landau–Siegel problem asks to prove that there are none, that is, that $\beta \le 1 - c/\log q$ for some absolute $c>0$ and all such zeros.

blocks.title: Real zeros near 1 make L(1, χ) small
blocks.body:
A zero close to $1$ and a small value at $1$ are two forms of the same phenomenon.

Lemma. Let $\chi$ be non-principal modulo $q \ge 8$. For $1 - \frac{1}{\log q} \le \sigma \le 1$ we have $|L'(\sigma,\chi)| \le C\log^2 q$ with an absolute constant $C$.

Proof. $L'(\sigma,\chi) = -\sum_n \chi(n)(\log n)n^{-\sigma}$. For $n \le q$ we have $n^{1-\sigma} \le q^{1/\log q} = e$, so the terms with $n \le q$ contribute at most $e\sum_{n\le q}\frac{\log n}{n} \le e\log q\,(1+\log q)$. For $n>q$ the function $t \mapsto (\log t)t^{-\sigma}$ is decreasing (since $q \ge 8 > e^{1/\sigma}$), so the partial-summation bound from [[l-functions]] gives at most $2\varphi(q)(\log q)q^{-\sigma} \le 2e\log q$. Adding up gives the claim.

Consequence. If $L(\beta,\chi)=0$ with $1-\frac{1}{\log q} \le \beta < 1$, the mean value theorem gives a $\sigma \in (\beta,1)$ with
$$L(1,\chi) = L(1,\chi) - L(\beta,\chi) = (1-\beta)L'(\sigma,\chi),\quad\text{so}\quad L(1,\chi) \le C(1-\beta)\log^2 q.$$
Read backwards: any lower bound for $L(1,\chi)$ gives a zero-free interval to the left of $1$,
$$1-\beta \ \ge\ \frac{L(1,\chi)}{C\log^2 q}.$$
For $D<-4$ the [[class-number-formula]] gives $L(1,\chi_D) = \pi h(D)/\sqrt{|D|} \ge \pi/\sqrt{|D|}$, so a real zero satisfies $1 - \beta \ge \pi/(C\sqrt{|D|}\log^2|D|)$. This is effective, but far weaker than the $c/\log q$ one would like. (For positive discriminants the formula $L(1,\chi_D) = 2h(D)\log\varepsilon_D/\sqrt D$ gives a bound of the same quality.)

blocks.title: Siegel's theorem (1935)
blocks.body:
For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a constant $c(\varepsilon)>0$ such that for every real primitive character $\chi$ modulo $q$,
$$L(1,\chi) > c(\varepsilon)\,q^{-\varepsilon}.$$
Consequently every real zero $\beta$ of $L(s,\chi)$ satisfies
$$1 - \beta \;\gg_\varepsilon\; q^{-\varepsilon},$$
and for $D<0$ the class number satisfies $h(D) \gg_\varepsilon |D|^{1/2-\varepsilon}$. For $\varepsilon < \frac12$ no established proof allows $c(\varepsilon)$ to be computed.

blocks.title: Why the constant cannot be computed
blocks.body:
The consequences follow from the main inequality: by the lemma, $1-\beta \ge c(\varepsilon)q^{-\varepsilon}/(C\log^2q)$, which is $\gg_\varepsilon q^{-2\varepsilon}$, and $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary; the class number bound is the class number formula. The interesting part is the main inequality. We describe the structure of the proof without the estimates (a short complete version is Goldfeld's, presented in Davenport, Chapter 21).

Take two distinct real primitive characters $\chi_1$, $\chi_2$ and form
$$F(s) = \zeta(s)L(s,\chi_1)L(s,\chi_2)L(s,\chi_1\chi_2).$$
This is the Dedekind zeta function of a biquadratic field. Its Dirichlet coefficients are non-negative, its first coefficient is $1$, and its residue at $s=1$ is $\lambda = L(1,\chi_1)L(1,\chi_2)L(1,\chi_1\chi_2)$. An inequality for Dirichlet series with these properties shows: if $F(\beta) \le 0$ for some $\beta$ close to $1$, then $\lambda$ cannot be much smaller than $(1-\beta)$ times a negative power $(q_1q_2)^{-O(1-\beta)}$.

Now split into two cases, depending on $\varepsilon$.

1. Some real primitive character $\chi_1$ has a real zero $\beta_1 \in (1-\varepsilon, 1)$. Fix one. For every other $\chi_2$ we have $F(\beta_1) = 0$, and the inequality gives a lower bound for $L(1,\chi_2)$ of the shape $c(\chi_1)\,q_2^{-O(\varepsilon)}$, where $c(\chi_1)$ depends on $q_1$ and $\beta_1$.
2. No real character has a zero in $(1-\varepsilon,1)$. Then $L(\beta,\chi) > 0$ on that interval for every real non-principal $\chi$ (it is positive at $\beta = 1$, as in the first example below, and has no zero in the interval), while $\zeta(\beta) < 0$ for $0<\beta<1$. So $F(\beta) < 0$ for every $\beta \in (1-\varepsilon,1)$, and the inequality again bounds $L(1,\chi_2)$ from below.

In both cases $L(1,\chi) \gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$. But in case 1 the constant depends on the character $\chi_1$, and we do not know whether case 1 happens at all, let alone which $\chi_1$ to take. That is the source of the ineffectivity: the proof is a proof by cases where one case may be empty and the other has an unknown parameter.

A partial remedy is due to Tatuzawa (1951): the inequality holds with an explicitly computable constant for all real primitive characters with at most one exception. Landau had earlier shown a related repulsion: two distinct real primitive characters cannot both have real zeros very close to $1$; there is an absolute $c$ with $\min(\beta_1,\beta_2) \le 1 - c/\log(q_1q_2)$.

blocks.title: What a Siegel zero would do
blocks.body:
1. Primes in progressions. In the explicit formula for primes in progressions modulo $q$, an exceptional zero $\beta_1$ of $L(s,\chi_1)$ contributes a secondary term, roughly
$$\psi(x;q,a) \approx \frac{x}{\varphi(q)}\bigl(1 - \chi_1(a)\,x^{\beta_1-1}\bigr).$$
If $\beta_1$ is very close to $1$, then $x^{\beta_1-1}$ stays close to $1$ for a long range of $x$: classes with $\chi_1(a) = 1$ are almost empty of primes and classes with $\chi_1(a) = -1$ receive almost twice their share. See [[siegel-walfisz]].

2. Class numbers. $h(D) = \sqrt{|D|}\,L(1,\chi_D)/\pi$ would be unusually small.

3. Repulsion of other zeros (the Deuring–Heilbronn phenomenon). An exceptional zero pushes the other zeros of all $L$-functions of nearby moduli away from $s=1$. This is so strong that a Siegel zero has some surprisingly good consequences: Heath-Brown (1983) proved that if Siegel zeros exist, then there are infinitely many twin primes.

That last point explains part of the difficulty: a Siegel zero leads to no visible contradiction, and in other respects it makes primes very regular.

blocks.title: Status
blocks.body:
Unconditionally, Siegel's theorem is the established general result, together with effective but much weaker bounds such as the one derived above. Under [[grh]] there are no Siegel zeros at all, since every non-trivial zero then has real part $\frac12$. Excluding them unconditionally, a statement much weaker than GRH, has been a central open problem since the 1930s.

On 6 October 2026, OpenAI released 372 result families on GitHub, among them a short paper claiming to exclude Siegel zeros. Three manuscripts were withdrawn the next day over a sign error. This is an AI-generated claim. Until it has been independently checked, the exclusion of Siegel zeros should be treated as claimed, not established; [[no-siegel]] tracks the claim.

blocks.title: Real zeros in the half-plane of convergence lie in (0, 1)
blocks.body: Let $\chi$ be a real non-principal character. Show that $L(\sigma,\chi) > 0$ for all real $\sigma \ge 1$. Deduce that any real zero with $\sigma > 0$ (where the series converges) lies in $(0,1)$.
blocks.solution:
For $\sigma>1$, each Euler factor $(1-\chi(p)p^{-\sigma})^{-1}$ is a positive real number, because $\chi(p) \in \{-1,0,1\}$ and $p^{-\sigma}<1$. Equivalently, $L(\sigma,\chi) = e^{\ell(\sigma,\chi)}$ where $\ell(\sigma,\chi) = \sum_p\sum_k \chi(p)^k/(kp^{k\sigma})$ is real. So $L(\sigma,\chi) > 0$ for $\sigma>1$.

At $\sigma = 1$: $L(\sigma,\chi)$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, so $L(1,\chi) = \lim_{\sigma\to1^+}L(\sigma,\chi) \ge 0$, and Dirichlet's theorem says $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$. Hence $L(1,\chi)>0$. So a real zero with $\sigma>0$ must lie in $(0,1)$, and the question is whether it can approach $1$ from the left. (The analytic continuation of $L(s,\chi)$ does have real zeros with $\sigma \le 0$, the trivial zeros at $0$ or the negative integers, but those play no role here.)

blocks.title: How small is L(1, χ_D) in practice?
blocks.body: Find the smallest values of $L(1,\chi_D)$ over fundamental discriminants $-5000 < D < -4$, and look at $L(\sigma,\chi_{-163})$ for real $\sigma<1$.

blocks.title: The size of the effect
blocks.body: Suppose, hypothetically, that a real character $\chi_1$ modulo $q$ had a zero at $\beta_1 = 1 - \frac{1}{100\log q}$, and ignore all other zeros. Using the approximate formula above, what share of its expected number of primes would a class $a$ with $\chi_1(a) = 1$ receive at $x = q^{10}$?
blocks.solution: We have $x^{\beta_1 - 1} = \exp\bigl(-\frac{\log x}{100\log q}\bigr) = \exp(-\frac{10}{100}) = e^{-0.1} \approx 0.905$. So the class would receive about $1 - 0.905 \approx 0.095$ of its share $x/\varphi(q)$, and a class with $\chi_1(a) = -1$ about $1.905$ of its share. Only when $\log x$ is many times $100\log q$ does the distortion fade, so a zero of this strength would distort the primes modulo $q$ up to about $x = q^{100}$ and beyond, that is, for moduli as large as a fixed power of $x$. For moduli $q \le (\log x)^A$ Siegel's bound $1-\beta \gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$ shows the effect is negligible, but only with an ineffective constant: this is the content of [[siegel-walfisz]].

blocks.body:
- Siegel's bound is ineffective: it proves $h(D) \to \infty$ at a rate $|D|^{1/2-\varepsilon}$, but it cannot tell you from which $|D|$ on, say, $h(D) > 10$. Explicit class number tables come from other methods.
- A Siegel zero is not merely a zero off the critical line. Any real zero in $(\frac12,1)$ would contradict GRH, but a Siegel zero must be closer to $1$ than $c/\log q$. Excluding Siegel zeros is much weaker than GRH.
- In $1-\beta \gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$ the implied constant depends on $\varepsilon$ and is not computable; it is not an absolute constant.

Siegel's theorem feeds directly into the [[siegel-walfisz]] theorem on primes in progressions to moduli up to a power of $\log x$, and through it into [[bombieri-vinogradov]] and the [[ternary-goldbach]] problem; the ineffective constant propagates into all of them. The link with class numbers is the [[class-number-formula]]. The hoped-for result, that Siegel zeros do not exist, is the subject of [[no-siegel]]; it would follow from [[grh]]. Heath-Brown's theorem connects the problem to [[twin-primes]].

1. Show that if $L(1,\chi) \ge c/\log q$ for all real primitive $\chi$ with an absolute $c>0$, then every real zero satisfies $1-\beta \ge c'/\log^3 q$.
2. Let $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ be prime and $\chi(n) = \bigl(\frac{n}{p}\bigr)$. Using the Euler product heuristically, explain why a very small value of $L(1,\chi)$ suggests that $\chi(\ell) = -1$ for most small primes $\ell$.
3. In the two-case proof of Siegel's theorem, identify exactly which quantity the final constant depends on and why it cannot be bounded explicitly.
4. Check that $h(-163) = 1$ by listing the reduced forms of discriminant $-163$, and compare $L(1,\chi_{-163})$ with the lower bound $\pi/\sqrt{|D|}$.

sources.ref: D. R. Heath-Brown, Prime twins and Siegel zeros, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (1983)

blocks.body:
The prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions says that for a fixed modulus $q$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$, the primes up to $x$ are shared equally among the $\varphi(q)$ admissible classes. In applications the modulus is rarely fixed. In the circle method, for instance, one needs the count of primes $p \le x$ with $p \equiv a \pmod q$ for all $q$ up to a power of $\log x$ simultaneously, with an error that is small compared with $x/\varphi(q)$.

The Siegel–Walfisz theorem (Walfisz, 1936, building on Siegel's theorem of 1935) gives exactly this: equidistribution uniformly for $q \le (\log x)^A$, for any fixed $A$, with an error saving a factor $e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}$. It has a price: because it relies on [[siegel-zeros|Siegel's theorem]], the implied constant cannot be computed.

blocks.title: ψ(x; q, a)
blocks.body:
For $\gcd(a,q)=1$,
$$\psi(x;q,a) = \sum_{\substack{n \le x \\ n \equiv a \ (q)}}\Lambda(n),$$
where $\Lambda$ is the von Mangoldt function ($\Lambda(p^k) = \log p$, and $0$ on non-prime-powers). It counts primes $p \equiv a \pmod q$ up to $x$ with weight $\log p$, plus a negligible contribution $O(\sqrt x\log x)$ from higher prime powers; its expected size is $x/\varphi(q)$.

blocks.title: Reduction to characters and zeros
blocks.body:
Orthogonality of characters gives
$$\psi(x;q,a) = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\chi \bmod q}\overline\chi(a)\,\psi(x,\chi),\qquad \psi(x,\chi) = \sum_{n\le x}\chi(n)\Lambda(n).$$
For the principal character, $\psi(x,\chi_0)$ differs from $\psi(x)$ only by the prime powers dividing $q$, at most $O(\log q\log x)$, and the prime number theorem with the classical error term (see [[pnt]]) gives $\psi(x) = x + O(xe^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})$. So the task is to show that $\psi(x,\chi)$ is small for each $\chi \ne \chi_0$.

The [[explicit-formula]] expresses $\psi(x,\chi)$ through the zeros $\rho = \beta + i\gamma$ of $L(s,\chi)$. For a primitive non-principal $\chi$ modulo $q$ and $2 \le T \le \sqrt x$,
$$\psi(x,\chi) = -\sum_{|\gamma| \le T}\frac{x^\rho}{\rho} + O\Bigl(\frac{x\log^2(qx)}{T}\Bigr),$$
and passing to an imprimitive character changes $\psi(x,\chi)$ by $O(\log^2(qx))$. Each zero contributes $|x^\rho| = x^\beta$, so what matters is how far the zeros stay from the line $\beta = 1$.

The [[zero-free-region]] says that, apart from at most one exceptional real zero $\beta_1$ belonging to a real character $\chi_1$, all zeros with $|\gamma| \le T$ satisfy $\beta \le 1 - c/\log(qT)$. There are $O(T\log(qT))$ zeros up to height $T$. Take $T = e^{\sqrt{\log x}}$ and $q \le T$. A non-exceptional zero then contributes at most
$$x^{\beta} \le x\exp\Bigl(-\frac{c\log x}{\log(qT)}\Bigr) \le x\exp\Bigl(-\frac{c}{2}\sqrt{\log x}\Bigr),$$
and the truncation error is $O(xe^{-\sqrt{\log x}}\log^2 x)$. Balancing the two losses is what produces $\sqrt{\log x}$ in the exponent. Carrying this out carefully (Davenport, Chapter 20) gives the following.

blocks.title: Prime number theorem for progressions, first form
blocks.body:
There are absolute constants $c, c_1>0$ such that for $q \le \exp(c_1\sqrt{\log x})$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$,
$$\psi(x;q,a) = \frac{x}{\varphi(q)} - \frac{\overline{\chi_1}(a)\,x^{\beta_1}}{\varphi(q)\,\beta_1} + O\bigl(x\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\bigr),$$
where the middle term is present only if some real character $\chi_1$ modulo $q$ has an exceptional zero $\beta_1$. Everything here, including the constants, is effective. (Proof omitted.)

blocks.title: The Siegel–Walfisz theorem
blocks.body:
For every $A>0$ there is a constant $C_A$ such that for all $x \ge 2$, all $q \le (\log x)^A$ and all $a$ with $\gcd(a,q)=1$,
$$\psi(x; q, a) = \frac{x}{\varphi(q)} + O_A\bigl(x\, e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\bigr),$$
that is, the error is at most $C_A\,x\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}$, where $c>0$ is absolute. The constant $C_A$ is ineffective.

blocks.title: Proof from the first form and Siegel's theorem
blocks.body:
For $x$ larger than some $x_0(A)$ we have $(\log x)^A \le \exp(c_1\sqrt{\log x})$, so the first form applies; smaller $x$ can be absorbed into $C_A$. It remains to show that the exceptional term is small.

The zero $\beta_1$ belongs to a real character $\chi_1$ modulo $q$, induced by a primitive real character modulo some $q^* \mid q$, and $L(s,\chi_1)$ and $L(s,\chi_1^*)$ have the same zeros in $0<\sigma<1$. Siegel's theorem with $\varepsilon = 1/(4A)$ gives
$$1 - \beta_1 \ \ge\ c(\varepsilon)\,(q^*)^{-\varepsilon} \ \ge\ c(\varepsilon)\,q^{-1/(4A)} \ \ge\ c(\varepsilon)\,(\log x)^{-1/4}.$$
Since $\beta_1 > 1 - c/\log q$, we may assume $\beta_1 \ge \frac12$ (shrinking the absolute constant $c$ of the zero-free region if necessary). Hence
$$\frac{x^{\beta_1}}{\varphi(q)\beta_1} \le 2x\exp\bigl(-(1-\beta_1)\log x\bigr) \le 2x\exp\bigl(-c(\varepsilon)(\log x)^{3/4}\bigr).$$
Since $(\log x)^{3/4}$ grows faster than $\sqrt{\log x}$, there is a constant $C'_A$ with $\exp(-c(\varepsilon)(\log x)^{3/4}) \le C'_A\exp(-c\sqrt{\log x})$ for all $x \ge 2$. This proves the theorem. The constant $C'_A$ depends on $c(\varepsilon)$, which Siegel's theorem does not let us compute.

The choice $\varepsilon = 1/(4A)$ rather than $1/(2A)$ keeps the constant $c$ in the exponent absolute: with $\varepsilon = 1/(2A)$ one would get $\exp(-c(\varepsilon)\sqrt{\log x})$, with an unknown constant in the exponent.

blocks.title: Equivalent forms and the limits of the range
blocks.body:
By partial summation the theorem is equivalent to
$$\pi(x;q,a) = \frac{\operatorname{li}(x)}{\varphi(q)} + O_A\bigl(x\,e^{-c'\sqrt{\log x}}\bigr)\qquad (q \le (\log x)^A),$$
where $\pi(x;q,a)$ counts primes $p \le x$ with $p \equiv a \pmod q$. A weaker form that is often quoted, and is all that many applications need, is: for all $A, B > 0$,
$$\psi(x;q,a) = \frac{x}{\varphi(q)} + O_{A,B}\Bigl(\frac{x}{(\log x)^B}\Bigr)\qquad(q \le (\log x)^A).$$

Why only powers of $\log x$? Suppose $q$ is as large as $x^\delta$. Siegel's bound then only says $1 - \beta_1 \ge c(\varepsilon)x^{-\delta\varepsilon}$, and $x^{\beta_1 - 1} \le \exp(-c(\varepsilon)x^{-\delta\varepsilon}\log x)$, which does not tend to $0$. A possible exceptional zero could then make the term $x^{\beta_1}/\varphi(q)$ as large as the main term. Three other results fill in different parts of the picture.

1. Under [[grh]], $\psi(x;q,a) = x/\varphi(q) + O(\sqrt x\log^2 x)$ for all $q \le x$, which is non-trivial up to $q \le x^{1/2-\varepsilon}$.
2. The [[bombieri-vinogradov]] theorem gives an error of GRH quality on average over $q \le x^{1/2}(\log x)^{-B}$. Its proof uses Siegel–Walfisz for small moduli and the large sieve for the rest.
3. Upper bounds of the correct order hold for all $q < x$: this is the Brun–Titchmarsh inequality from [[selberg-sieve]].

blocks.title: Primes modulo 7 up to a million
blocks.body: Compute $\psi(10^6;7,a)$ and $\pi(10^6;7,a)$ for $a = 1,\dots,6$ and compare them with the predictions $10^6/6$ and $\operatorname{li}(10^6)/6$.
blocks.solution:
A direct computation gives
- $\psi(10^6;7,a) \approx 166560.3,\ 166518.7,\ 166676.6,\ 166586.3,\ 166683.2,\ 166547.9$ for $a = 1,\dots,6$, against $10^6/6 \approx 166666.7$. The largest deviation is about $148$ (at $a=2$), well below $\sqrt{10^6} = 1000$.
- $\pi(10^6;7,a) = 13063,\ 13065,\ 13105,\ 13069,\ 13105,\ 13090$, which together with the prime $7$ itself add up to $\pi(10^6) = 78498$. The prediction is $\operatorname{li}(10^6)/6 \approx 13104.6$.

Deviations of size about $\sqrt x$ are what GRH predicts. Siegel–Walfisz guarantees much less, an error $O(xe^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})$ with an unknown constant, but it does so uniformly in $q \le (\log x)^A$. A single numerical table can neither confirm nor refute an ineffective asymptotic statement.

blocks.title: The least prime in a progression
blocks.body: Let $p(q,a)$ be the least prime $p \equiv a \pmod q$. Deduce from the Siegel–Walfisz theorem that for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $p(q,a) \le \exp(q^{\varepsilon})$ for all $q \ge q_0(\varepsilon)$ and all $a$ coprime to $q$. Is the threshold $q_0(\varepsilon)$ computable?
blocks.solution:
Let $A = 1/\varepsilon$ and $x = \exp(q^{\varepsilon})$, so that $q = (\log x)^A$ and the theorem applies. Higher prime powers $p^k \le x$ with $k \ge 2$ contribute at most $O(\sqrt x\log^2 x)$ to $\psi(x;q,a)$. So the contribution of primes is at least
$$\frac{x}{\varphi(q)} - C_Ax\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}} - O(\sqrt x\log^2x) \ \ge\ \frac{x}{q}\Bigl(1 - C_Aq\,e^{-c\,q^{\varepsilon/2}}\Bigr) - O(\sqrt x\log^2 x),$$
using $\sqrt{\log x} = q^{\varepsilon/2}$. The bracket tends to $1$ as $q \to \infty$, and $\sqrt x\log^2 x$ is negligible against $x/q$ because $x = \exp(q^\varepsilon)$ grows much faster than any power of $q$. So for $q \ge q_0(\varepsilon)$ there is a prime $p \le x$ with $p \equiv a \pmod q$.

Since $C_A$ is ineffective, so is $q_0(\varepsilon)$. This bound is very weak: Linnik (1944) proved, by quite different methods, that $p(q,a) \le C q^{L}$ for absolute, effectively computable constants $C$ and $L$. In practice the least prime is much smaller still; for every $2 \le q \le 300$ and every $a$ coprime to $q$ one finds $p(q,a) < q^2$, the worst ratio $p(q,a)/q^2$ being $7/9$ at $q=3$, $a=1$.

blocks.body:
- The hypothesis $\gcd(a,q)=1$ is required.
- Ineffectivity is real: from Siegel–Walfisz alone one cannot extract an explicit $x_0$ beyond which, say, every progression modulo $q \le \log x$ contains a prime up to $x$. Results that need explicit thresholds (such as explicit forms of the three-primes theorem) must treat the possible exceptional zero separately.
- The range $q \le (\log x)^A$ is tiny. Most sieve applications need moduli up to a power of $x$, which is why [[bombieri-vinogradov]] is needed.
- The two constants play different roles: $c$ in the exponent is absolute, while the implied constant depends on $A$ and is ineffective.
- Relative to the main term the error is $\varphi(q)\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}} \le (\log x)^Ae^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}$, which tends to $0$; outside the range no such conclusion follows.

In Vinogradov's proof of the [[ternary-goldbach]] theorem by the [[circle-method]], the major arcs require exactly the distribution of primes in progressions to moduli up to a power of $\log x$, which Siegel–Walfisz supplies. In the [[bombieri-vinogradov]] theorem it handles the small moduli, and it appears as the standard hypothesis ("the sequence satisfies a Siegel–Walfisz condition") in many results on bilinear forms and sieves. An exclusion of Siegel zeros ([[no-siegel]]) would make these results effective and would extend the range of uniformity.

blocks.body:
To list the primes up to $100$, cross out the multiples of $2, 3, 5, 7$; what survives, apart from $1$, are the primes between $10$ and $100$. This is the sieve of Eratosthenes. Written as an inclusion–exclusion formula it becomes an exact identity for $\pi(x)$, due to Legendre. The identity is useless as it stands, because its error terms swamp the main term, but the idea behind it is right: many questions about primes ask how many integers survive after we remove a few residue classes modulo each small prime.

Twin primes are the model case. A pair $n, n+2$ consists of two primes (beyond the small ones) exactly when $n(n+2)$ has no small prime factor. In 1919 Viggo Brun found how to truncate inclusion–exclusion so that the error terms stay under control, and proved that the sum of the reciprocals of the twin primes converges: the first substantial theorem about twin primes, and the beginning of modern sieve theory.

blocks.title: Inclusion–exclusion with the Möbius function
blocks.body:
For $z \ge 2$ let $P(z) = \prod_{p \le z}p$, the product of the primes up to $z$. For a finite set $\mathcal{A}$ of positive integers define the sifted count
$$S(\mathcal{A},z) = \#\{n \in \mathcal{A} : \gcd(n, P(z)) = 1\},$$
and for $d \mid P(z)$ let $\mathcal{A}_d = \{n \in \mathcal{A} : d \mid n\}$.

The basic fact about the Möbius function (see [[mobius]]) is that $\sum_{d\mid m}\mu(d)$ equals $1$ if $m=1$ and $0$ otherwise. Applied to $m = \gcd(n,P(z))$, whose divisors are exactly the $d \mid P(z)$ with $d \mid n$,
$$S(\mathcal{A},z) = \sum_{n\in\mathcal{A}}\ \sum_{\substack{d \mid P(z)\\ d \mid n}}\mu(d) = \sum_{d \mid P(z)}\mu(d)\,|\mathcal{A}_d|.$$
This is inclusion–exclusion: add all elements, subtract those divisible by each $p$, add back those divisible by each $pq$, and so on.

blocks.title: Legendre's identity
blocks.body:
For $x \ge 1$,
$$\pi(x) - \pi(\sqrt x) + 1 = \sum_{d \mid P(\sqrt x)} \mu(d) \Bigl\lfloor \frac{x}{d} \Bigr\rfloor.$$

Take $\mathcal{A} = \{1, 2, \dots, \lfloor x\rfloor\}$ and $z = \sqrt x$, so that $|\mathcal{A}_d| = \lfloor x/d\rfloor$ and the right side is $S(\mathcal{A},\sqrt x)$. An integer $1 < n \le x$ with no prime factor $\le \sqrt x$ must be prime, since a composite $n$ has a prime factor at most $\sqrt n \le \sqrt x$; conversely every prime $p$ with $\sqrt x < p \le x$ survives. Together with $n = 1$, the survivors number $1 + \pi(x) - \pi(\sqrt x)$.

blocks.title: Why the identity alone fails
blocks.body:
Write $\lfloor x/d \rfloor = x/d - \{x/d\}$. Since $\sum_{d\mid P(z)}\mu(d)/d = \prod_{p\le z}(1 - 1/p)$,
$$S(\mathcal{A},z) = x\prod_{p \le z}\Bigl(1 - \frac1p\Bigr) + E,\qquad |E| \le 2^{\pi(z)}.$$
The main term is what probability suggests: a random integer avoids each prime $p$ with probability $1 - 1/p$. But the error bound has one term for each divisor of $P(z)$, and for $z = \sqrt x$ there are $2^{\pi(\sqrt x)}$ of them, vastly more than $x$.

Worse, the main term is not even asymptotically right. By [[mertens]], $\prod_{p\le z}(1-1/p) \sim e^{-\gamma}/\log z$, so with $z = \sqrt x$ the main term is asymptotic to $2e^{-\gamma}x/\log x \approx 1.1229\,x/\log x$, while the prime number theorem gives $\pi(x) \sim x/\log x$. The errors $\{x/d\}$ do not cancel; they add up to a quantity comparable with the main term.

What does work is to sieve only by small primes. If $z$ is so small that $2^{\pi(z)}$ is negligible, the main term dominates, and every prime $p > z$ up to $x$ is among the survivors.

blocks.title: Legendre's identity at x = 100
blocks.body: Evaluate the right side of Legendre's identity for $x = 100$ and check it against $\pi(100) = 25$.
blocks.solution:
Here $P(10) = 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$. Grouping the divisors by their number of prime factors:
- $d = 1$: $100$.
- one prime: $\lfloor 100/2\rfloor + \lfloor 100/3\rfloor + \lfloor 100/5\rfloor + \lfloor 100/7\rfloor = 50 + 33 + 20 + 14 = 117$.
- two primes ($6, 10, 14, 15, 21, 35$): $16 + 10 + 7 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 45$.
- three primes ($30, 42, 70, 105$): $3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 6$.
- $d = 210$: $0$.

So the sum is $100 - 117 + 45 - 6 + 0 = 22$. On the left, $\pi(100) - \pi(10) + 1 = 25 - 4 + 1 = 22$.

blocks.title: Legendre's upper bound
blocks.body: Show that $\pi(x) \ll x/\log\log x$ by sieving only with the primes up to $z = \log x$.
blocks.solution:
Every prime $p \le x$ either satisfies $p \le z$ or survives the sieve by the primes up to $z$. Hence
$$\pi(x) \le z + S(\mathcal{A},z) \le z + x\prod_{p\le z}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr) + 2^{\pi(z)}.$$
With $z = \log x$ we have $2^{\pi(z)} \le 2^{z} = x^{\log 2} \approx x^{0.693}$, and by Mertens' theorem $\prod_{p \le z}(1-1/p) \ll 1/\log z = 1/\log\log x$. All three terms are $O(x/\log\log x)$.

This already shows that the primes have density $0$, but it is far from the truth $x/\log x$. The loss comes from the crude treatment of the $2^{\pi(z)}$ error terms, which forces $z$ to be tiny.

blocks.title: Brun's idea: truncate
blocks.body: Brun's observation is that inclusion–exclusion, cut off after the terms with at most $r$ prime factors, gives one-sided bounds. Write $\omega(d)$ for the number of prime factors of $d$.

blocks.title: Bonferroni inequalities
blocks.body:
Let $m$ be a squarefree integer with $k = \omega(m) \ge 1$. Then for every $r \ge 0$,
$$\sum_{\substack{d \mid m\\ \omega(d) \le r}}\mu(d) = \sum_{j=0}^{r}(-1)^j\binom{k}{j} = (-1)^r\binom{k-1}{r}.$$
Hence the truncated sum is $\ge 0$ for even $r$ and $\le 0$ for odd $r$, while for $m = 1$ it equals $1$. Consequently, for every $r$,
$$(-1)^r\sum_{\substack{d \mid P(z) \\ \omega(d) \le r}}\mu(d)|\mathcal{A}_d| \ \ge\ (-1)^r S(\mathcal{A},z).$$

The first equality holds because $m$ has $\binom kj$ divisors with $j$ prime factors, each with $\mu(d) = (-1)^j$. The second is proved by induction on $r$: it holds for $r = 0$, and using Pascal's rule $\binom kr = \binom{k-1}{r} + \binom{k-1}{r-1}$,
$$(-1)^{r-1}\binom{k-1}{r-1} + (-1)^r\binom{k}{r} = (-1)^r\Bigl(\binom kr - \binom{k-1}{r-1}\Bigr) = (-1)^r\binom{k-1}{r}.$$
For the consequence, apply this with $m = \gcd(n,P(z))$ for each $n \in \mathcal{A}$ and sum. Elements with $m=1$ contribute exactly $1$ to both sides; the others contribute $(-1)^r\binom{k-1}{r}$ to the truncated sum, which has sign $(-1)^r$ or is $0$.

blocks.title: Truncation in practice
blocks.body: How many integers $1 \le n \le 1000$ are coprime to $210 = 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$? Compute the truncated sums for $r = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ and check the alternating bounds.

blocks.title: Brun's theorem
blocks.body:
For twin primes take $\mathcal{A} = \{n(n+2) : n \le x\}$. For an odd prime $p$, the condition $p \mid n(n+2)$ holds for two residue classes $n \equiv 0, -2 \pmod p$, and for $p=2$ for one class. So for squarefree $d$,
$$|\mathcal{A}_d| = x\frac{\rho(d)}{d} + R_d,\qquad |R_d| \le \rho(d),$$
where $\rho$ is multiplicative with $\rho(2) = 1$ and $\rho(p) = 2$ for odd $p$. The expected proportion of survivors is $\prod_{p\le z}(1 - \rho(p)/p)$, which by Mertens' theorem is of order $1/(\log z)^2$.

Brun's pure sieve takes an even $r$ and bounds $S(\mathcal{A},z)$ above by the truncated sum. Three quantities have to be controlled:
1. the main term $x\prod_{p\le z}(1 - \rho(p)/p) \asymp x/(\log z)^2$;
2. the truncation loss in the main term, which is at most $x\sum_{\omega(d) = r+1}\rho(d)/d \le x\,\frac{(\sum_{p\le z}\rho(p)/p)^{r+1}}{(r+1)!}$, by the Bonferroni inequalities for independent events of probabilities $\rho(p)/p$; here $\sum_{p\le z}\rho(p)/p = 2\log\log z + O(1)$;
3. the remainders, at most $\sum_{\omega(d)\le r}\rho(d) \le (1+2\pi(z))^r$.

Taking $r$ a large constant multiple of $\log\log x$ makes the second term small because of the factorial, and taking $\log z$ a small constant times $\log x/\log\log x$ keeps $z^r$, and hence the third term, below $\sqrt x$. The main term is then $\asymp x(\log\log x)^2/(\log x)^2$. Since the number $\pi_2(x)$ of $n \le x$ with $n$ and $n+2$ both prime is at most $z + S(\mathcal{A},z)$, this gives
$$\pi_2(x) \ll \frac{x(\log\log x)^2}{(\log x)^2}.$$
More elaborate sieves (Brun's general sieve, or the [[selberg-sieve]]) remove the factor $(\log\log x)^2$ and give the upper bound $\pi_2(x) \ll x/(\log x)^2$, which is the conjectured order of magnitude.

blocks.title: Brun's theorem (1919)
blocks.body:
The sum of the reciprocals of the twin primes converges:
$$\sum_{\substack{p\\ p+2 \text{ prime}}}\Bigl(\frac1p + \frac1{p+2}\Bigr) < \infty.$$

blocks.title: Proof from the upper bound
blocks.body:
It suffices to show $\sum 1/p < \infty$ over primes $p$ with $p+2$ prime, since $1/(p+2) < 1/p$. By partial summation,
$$\sum_{\substack{p \le x\\ p+2\text{ prime}}}\frac1p = \frac{\pi_2(x)}{x} + \int_2^x\frac{\pi_2(t)}{t^2}\,dt \ \ll\ 1 + \int_3^x\frac{(\log\log t)^2}{t(\log t)^2}\,dt.$$
With $u = \log t$ the integral becomes $\int (\log u)^2/u^2\,du$, which converges as $u \to \infty$. So the partial sums are bounded.

blocks.title: How slowly Brun's sum converges
blocks.body: Compute the number of twin prime pairs $(p, p+2)$ with $p \le 10^6$ and the partial sum of $\frac1p + \frac{1}{p+2}$ over them. Estimate the tail heuristically, assuming the Hardy–Littlewood prediction $\pi_2(t) \approx 2C_2t/(\log t)^2$ with $C_2 = \prod_{p>2}\bigl(1 - \frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\bigr) \approx 0.6602$.
blocks.solution:
There are $8169$ such pairs, and the partial sum is approximately $1.7108$. Under the heuristic, each pair contributes about $2/t$ and the pairs near $t$ have density $2C_2/(\log t)^2$, so the tail beyond $x$ is about
$$\int_x^\infty\frac{2}{t}\cdot\frac{2C_2}{(\log t)^2}\,dt = \frac{4C_2}{\log x} \approx \frac{4 \cdot 0.6602}{13.8155} \approx 0.191.$$
This suggests a total of about $1.902$, in line with the much larger computations that estimate Brun's constant at about $1.902$. Even at $x = 10^6$ about a tenth of the sum is still missing, and the tail decays only like $1/\log x$.

blocks.body:
- In Legendre's identity $P(\sqrt x)$ must include the primes equal to $\sqrt x$. With $P(z) = \prod_{p<z}p$ the identity fails at $x = p^2$.
- The probabilistic main term $x\prod_{p\le\sqrt x}(1-1/p)$ is not asymptotic to $\pi(x)$: it is about $2e^{-\gamma} \approx 1.12$ times too large in the limit. (At $x = 10^8$ it is about $6\,088\,469$, against $\pi(10^8) - \pi(10^4) + 1 = 5\,760\,227$.)
- Brun's theorem does not say that there are finitely many twin primes; a convergent sum is consistent with infinitely many terms (and the conjecture is that there are infinitely many).
- The alternating bounds hold for truncation by the number of prime factors $\omega(d)$. Truncating by the size of $d$ has no such sign property.
- Sieves have a built-in limitation, the parity problem identified by Selberg: information of the form $|\mathcal{A}_d| \approx Xg(d)$ alone cannot distinguish integers with an even number of prime factors from those with an odd number. Pure sieve methods cannot prove the twin prime conjecture.

Brun's combinatorial truncation was replaced in many problems by optimized weights: [[selberg-sieve]] chooses the weights by minimizing a quadratic form, and the [[large-sieve]] gives a different, analytic way to bound sifted sets. Sieve upper bounds of the right order of magnitude for twin primes and for Goldbach representations are standard tools for [[twin-primes]], [[goldbach]] and, more generally, [[prime-patterns]]. Combined with results on primes in progressions, sieve ideas lead to Chen's theorem (every large even number is a prime plus a number with at most two prime factors, 1973) and, in a refined form, to [[bounded-gaps]].

4. Show that the number of $n \le x$ such that neither $n$ nor $n+2$ has a prime factor $\le \log x$ is $O(x/(\log\log x)^2)$.

blocks.body:
Brun's sieve (see [[sieve-basics]]) obtains upper bounds by cutting inclusion–exclusion off at a carefully chosen point. The bounds have the right order of magnitude, but the combinatorics is intricate and the constants are poor. In 1947 Atle Selberg replaced the whole construction by a single observation: a square is never negative. If we bound the indicator of "no small prime factor" by a square of a sum of free weights $\lambda_d$, every choice of weights gives an upper bound, and the best weights can be found by minimizing a quadratic form.

The result is a sieve that is simple to set up, gives the sharpest known constants in many problems (for example, at most $(2+o(1))\,y/\log y$ primes in any interval of length $y$), and, through the work of Goldston, Pintz, Yıldırım and then Maynard, became the engine behind bounded gaps between primes.

blocks.title: The setting
blocks.body:
We keep the notation of [[sieve-basics]]: $\mathcal{A}$ is a finite set of integers, $P(z) = \prod_{p\le z}p$, $S(\mathcal{A},z)$ counts the elements of $\mathcal{A}$ coprime to $P(z)$, and $\mathcal{A}_d$ is the set of elements divisible by $d$. We assume that for squarefree $d \mid P(z)$,
$$|\mathcal{A}_d| = X g(d) + r_d,$$
where $X$ approximates $|\mathcal{A}|$, $g$ is multiplicative with $0 < g(p) < 1$, and $r_d$ is a remainder we hope is small. For the integers in an interval of length $y$, $X = y$, $g(d) = 1/d$ and $|r_d| \le 1$.

blocks.title: Selberg's upper bound
blocks.body:
Let $\lambda_d$ be any real numbers indexed by squarefree $d \mid P(z)$, with $\lambda_1 = 1$ and $\lambda_d = 0$ for $d > \sqrt D$, where $D$ is a parameter called the level. For each $n$,
$$\Bigl(\sum_{d \mid \gcd(n,P(z))}\lambda_d\Bigr)^2 \ \ge\ \begin{cases}1 & \gcd(n,P(z)) = 1,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$
because in the first case the inner sum is just $\lambda_1 = 1$, and in the second it is a square. Summing over $n \in \mathcal{A}$ and expanding the square,
$$S(\mathcal{A},z) \le \sum_{n \in\mathcal{A}}\Bigl(\sum_{d \mid \gcd(n,P(z))}\lambda_d\Bigr)^2 = \sum_{d_1,d_2}\lambda_{d_1}\lambda_{d_2}\,|\mathcal{A}_{[d_1,d_2]}| = X\,Q(\lambda) + R(\lambda),$$
where $[d_1,d_2]$ is the least common multiple, and
$$Q(\lambda) = \sum_{d_1,d_2}\lambda_{d_1}\lambda_{d_2}\,g([d_1,d_2]),\qquad R(\lambda) = \sum_{d_1,d_2}\lambda_{d_1}\lambda_{d_2}\,r_{[d_1,d_2]}.$$
Since $d_1, d_2 \le \sqrt D$, only remainders $r_d$ with $d \le D$ appear. The idea is to choose the $\lambda_d$ to minimize the quadratic form $Q$ subject to $\lambda_1 = 1$, and then check that the remainder stays small.

blocks.title: Diagonalizing the quadratic form
blocks.body:
For squarefree $d_1,d_2$ we have $g([d_1,d_2]) = g(d_1)g(d_2)/g(\gcd(d_1,d_2))$. Define a multiplicative function $h$ on squarefree numbers by $h(p) = \frac{1}{g(p)} - 1 = \frac{1-g(p)}{g(p)} > 0$. Then $\frac{1}{g(m)} = \prod_{p\mid m}(1 + h(p)) = \sum_{e \mid m}h(e)$, and therefore
$$Q(\lambda) = \sum_{d_1,d_2}\lambda_{d_1}g(d_1)\lambda_{d_2}g(d_2)\sum_{e \mid \gcd(d_1,d_2)}h(e) = \sum_{e}h(e)\,y_e^2,\qquad y_e = \sum_{d:\ e\mid d}\lambda_d\,g(d).$$
The quadratic form is now a sum of squares. Möbius inversion over the divisors of $P(z)$ recovers the weights from the new variables: $\lambda_d\,g(d) = \sum_{e:\ d \mid e}\mu(e/d)\,y_e$. In particular $y_e = 0$ for $e > \sqrt D$, and the constraint $\lambda_1 = 1$ becomes
$$\sum_{e}\mu(e)\,y_e = 1.$$
By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$1 = \Bigl(\sum_e\mu(e)y_e\Bigr)^2 \le \Bigl(\sum_e h(e)y_e^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_e\frac{1}{h(e)}\Bigr) = Q(\lambda)\,G,\qquad G = \sum_{\substack{e \mid P(z)\\ e \le \sqrt D}}\frac{1}{h(e)},$$
with equality when $y_e$ is proportional to $\mu(e)/h(e)$, namely $y_e = \mu(e)/(h(e)G)$. So the minimum of $Q$ is exactly $1/G$. Note that $1/h(e) = \prod_{p \mid e}\frac{g(p)}{1-g(p)}$.

blocks.title: The Selberg sieve
blocks.body:
With the notation above, for every $z \ge 2$ and $D \ge 1$,
$$S(\mathcal{A},z) \ \le\ \frac{X}{G} + \sum_{\substack{d_1,d_2 \mid P(z)\\ d_1,d_2 \le \sqrt D}}\bigl|r_{[d_1,d_2]}\bigr|,\qquad G = \sum_{\substack{e \mid P(z)\\ e\le\sqrt D}}\ \prod_{p\mid e}\frac{g(p)}{1-g(p)}.$$

Take the optimal weights, so that $Q(\lambda) = 1/G$. It remains to show $|\lambda_d| \le 1$, which gives $|R(\lambda)| \le \sum|r_{[d_1,d_2]}|$.

From $\lambda_d g(d) = \sum_{d\mid e}\mu(e/d)y_e$ and $y_e = \mu(e)/(h(e)G)$, writing $e = dm$ with $\gcd(m,d) = 1$ (as $e$ is squarefree) and using $\mu(m)\mu(dm) = \mu(d)\mu(m)^2$,
$$\lambda_d = \frac{\mu(d)}{g(d)h(d)\,G}\sum_{\substack{m \le \sqrt D/d,\ m \mid P(z)\\ \gcd(m,d) = 1}}\frac{1}{h(m)}.$$
Now split the sum defining $G$ according to $\gcd(e,d)$: every pair $(\ell,m)$ with $\ell \mid d$, $\gcd(m,d)=1$, $m \mid P(z)$ and $m \le \sqrt D/d$ gives a distinct $e = \ell m \le \sqrt D$ dividing $P(z)$, so
$$G \ \ge\ \sum_{\ell\mid d}\frac{1}{h(\ell)}\sum_{\substack{m \le \sqrt D/d,\ m\mid P(z)\\ \gcd(m,d)=1}}\frac{1}{h(m)} = \frac{1}{g(d)h(d)}\sum_{\substack{m \le \sqrt D/d,\ m\mid P(z)\\ \gcd(m,d)=1}}\frac{1}{h(m)},$$
because $$\sum_{\ell \mid d}\frac{1}{h(\ell)} = \prod_{p \mid d}\Bigl(1 + \frac{g(p)}{1-g(p)}\Bigr) = \prod_{p\mid d}\frac{1}{1-g(p)} = \frac{1}{g(d)h(d)}$$. Comparing the two displays gives $|\lambda_d| \le 1$.

blocks.title: Primes in short intervals (Brun–Titchmarsh type)
blocks.body:
For $y \ge 3$ and every $x \ge 0$,
$$\pi(x+y) - \pi(x) \ \le\ \frac{2y}{\log y} + O\Bigl(\frac{y\log\log y}{(\log y)^2}\Bigr),$$
with an absolute implied constant. In particular $\pi(x+y)-\pi(x) \le (2+o(1))\,y/\log y$ uniformly in $x$.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the integers in $(x, x+y]$, so $X = y$, $g(d) = 1/d$, $|r_d| \le 1$. Then $\frac{g(p)}{1-g(p)} = \frac{1}{p-1}$ and $\prod_{p\mid e}\frac{1}{p-1} = \frac{1}{\varphi(e)}$ for squarefree $e$. Choose $z = \sqrt D$; then every squarefree $e \le \sqrt D$ divides $P(z)$, and
$$G = \sum_{e \le \sqrt D}\frac{\mu^2(e)}{\varphi(e)} \ \ge\ \log\sqrt D.$$
To see the last inequality, expand $\frac{1}{\varphi(e)} = \frac1e\prod_{p\mid e}\bigl(1 + \frac1p + \frac1{p^2} + \cdots\bigr)$ for squarefree $e$: the sum becomes $\sum 1/n$ over all $n$ whose largest squarefree divisor is at most $\sqrt D$, which includes every $n \le \sqrt D$, and $\sum_{n \le t}1/n \ge \log t$.

The remainder is at most $\bigl(\sum_{d\le\sqrt D}1\bigr)^2 \le D$. A prime in $(x,x+y]$ either is at most $z$ or has no prime factor $\le z$, so
$$\pi(x+y) - \pi(x) \le z + S(\mathcal{A},z) \le \sqrt D + \frac{2y}{\log D} + D.$$
Take $D = y/(\log y)^2$. Then $\log D = \log y - 2\log\log y$, so $\frac{2y}{\log D} = \frac{2y}{\log y} + O\bigl(\frac{y\log\log y}{(\log y)^2}\bigr)$, and $D + \sqrt D = O(y/(\log y)^2)$.

blocks.title: The constant 2, and arithmetic progressions
blocks.body:
The same argument applied to $\{n \le x : n \equiv a \pmod q\}$ gives the Brun–Titchmarsh inequality
$$\pi(x;q,a) \le \frac{(2+o(1))\,x}{\varphi(q)\log(x/q)}\qquad (q < x),$$
valid for all moduli, in contrast to the asymptotic results of [[siegel-walfisz]] for small moduli. Montgomery and Vaughan (1973) showed, using the sharp form of the [[large-sieve]], that the $o(1)$ can be removed: $\pi(x;q,a) \le 2x/(\varphi(q)\log(x/q))$ for $q<x$, and $\pi(x+y)-\pi(x) \le 2y/\log y$ for $y>1$.

The prime number theorem suggests the truth is about $y/\log y$, half the bound. The factor $2$ is not an artefact of Selberg's method that a cleverer choice of weights could remove: it is the parity problem of sieve theory, which shows that sieve information alone cannot do better. In the other direction, a Siegel zero would give the classes with $\chi_1(a) = -1$ almost twice their expected share of primes over a long range of $x$, close to this bound; this is why improving the constant $2$ uniformly in $q$ is tied to excluding [[siegel-zeros]].

blocks.title: From Selberg to bounded gaps
blocks.body:
In the twin prime problem the weights $(\sum_{d \mid n(n+2)}\lambda_d)^2$ give an upper bound of the right order $x/(\log x)^2$, though with a larger constant than the conjectured one. The decisive new use of Selberg's idea was different. Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım (2005) used weights of the form $\bigl(\sum_{d \mid (n+h_1)\cdots(n+h_k)}\lambda_d\bigr)^2$, with $\lambda_d$ given by a smooth function of $\log d/\log R$, not to count primes but to detect $n$ for which several of $n+h_1, \dots, n+h_k$ are prime at once.

Maynard (2013) let the weights depend on the divisors of each $n+h_i$ separately, $\lambda_{d_1,\dots,d_k}$ with $d_i \mid n+h_i$, and optimized a quadratic form in a function of $k$ variables. This multidimensional Selberg sieve showed that $\liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n) \le 600$, independently of Zhang's earlier breakthrough. The Polymath8 project lowered the bound to $246$. See [[bounded-gaps]].

blocks.title: A sieve problem in miniature
blocks.body:
Sieve the integers by $2$ and $3$ only, using weights supported on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ (that is, $\sqrt D = 3$, so $\lambda_6 = 0$). Find the $\lambda_2, \lambda_3$ that minimize
$$Q(\lambda) = \sum_{d_1,d_2 \in\{1,2,3\}}\frac{\lambda_{d_1}\lambda_{d_2}}{[d_1,d_2]},\qquad \lambda_1 = 1,$$
and compare the resulting upper bound for the density of integers coprime to $6$ with the true value $\frac13$ and with the choice $\lambda_d = \mu(d)$.
blocks.solution:
Expanding,
$$Q = 1 + \lambda_2 + \tfrac23\lambda_3 + \tfrac12\lambda_2^2 + \tfrac13\lambda_3^2 + \tfrac13\lambda_2\lambda_3.$$
With $g(d) = 1/d$ we have $h(e) = \varphi(e)$, so $G = \frac{1}{\varphi(1)} + \frac{1}{\varphi(2)} + \frac{1}{\varphi(3)} = 1 + 1 + \frac12 = \frac52$ and the minimum is $\frac{1}{G} = \frac25$. The optimal $y_e = \mu(e)/(\varphi(e)G)$ are $y_1 = \frac25$, $y_2 = -\frac25$, $y_3 = -\frac15$, and $\lambda_d = d\,y_d$ for $d = 2, 3$ gives $\lambda_2 = -\frac45$, $\lambda_3 = -\frac35$. As a check, $\lambda_1 = y_1 - y_2 - y_3 = 1$, and substituting into $Q$ gives
$$1 - \tfrac45 - \tfrac25 + \tfrac{8}{25} + \tfrac{3}{25} + \tfrac{4}{25} = \tfrac25.$$
Alternatively, setting the partial derivatives of $Q$ to zero gives the linear system $\lambda_2 + \frac13\lambda_3 = -1$, $\frac13\lambda_2 + \frac23\lambda_3 = -\frac23$, with the same solution.

So the density of integers coprime to $6$ is at most $\frac25 = 0.4$. The choice $\lambda_2 = \lambda_3 = -1$ (inclusion–exclusion with the term $d=6$ missing) gives $Q = \frac12$, worse. The true density is $\frac13$, and it is attained only when $6$ is allowed in the support: with support $\{1,2,3,6\}$ one gets $G = 3$ and $Q = \frac13$, the full inclusion–exclusion. A smaller level costs accuracy, and in return keeps the remainder terms under control.

blocks.title: Checking the short-interval bound
blocks.body: For $y = 1000$, compare the bound $2y/\log y$ with the largest number of primes in an interval $(x, x+1000]$ for $0 \le x \le 10^6$.
blocks.solution: Here $2y/\log y \approx 289.5$. The maximum of $\pi(x+1000) - \pi(x)$ over $0 \le x \le 10^6$ is $168 = \pi(1000)$, attained at $x = 0$; over $10^5 \le x \le 10^6$ it is $101$. The prime number theorem predicts about $1000/\log x$ primes in such an interval ($\approx 86.9$ at $x = 10^5$), so the bound is off by a factor of about $3$ to $4$ in this range ($289.5/86.9 \approx 3.3$ at $x = 10^5$, and $1000/\log 10^6 \approx 72.4$ gives $4.0$ at $x = 10^6$). Only a factor $2$ comes from the constant; the rest comes from $\log y$ in the bound against $\log x$ in the truth, a loss that any bound uniform in $x$ must accept. Its value lies in the uniformity: it holds for every $x$, including ranges far beyond the reach of any computation and far beyond the reach of the prime number theorem with error term.

blocks.body:
- The Selberg sieve, as presented, gives only upper bounds, since it rests on the positivity of a square. Lower bounds need other devices (combining with Buchstab's identity, or the beta sieve).
- The assumption $g(p)<1$ matters: if $g(p) = 1$, essentially every element is divisible by $p$ and the sifted set is empty or tiny; the function $h$ would vanish.
- The level $D$ must be chosen so that the remainder sum over $d_1,d_2 \le \sqrt D$ is smaller than the main term. Taking $D$ as large as $X$ makes the remainder as large as the main term.
- The optimal weights are not $\mu(d)$ truncated; they are smoother. In the interval example they behave like $\mu(d)\log(\sqrt D/d)/\log\sqrt D$ for most $d$.

The Selberg sieve is the starting point for the multidimensional sieve behind [[bounded-gaps]], and its upper bounds are used throughout the study of [[twin-primes]] and [[prime-patterns]]. Its sharpest form, and the Brun–Titchmarsh inequality without the $o(1)$, come from the [[large-sieve]]; the level of distribution $D$ it can use for primes is what the [[bombieri-vinogradov]] theorem supplies. The parity limitation of the constant $2$ is tied to the problem of [[siegel-zeros]].

1. Repeat the miniature example with support $\{1,2,3,5\}$ and $g(d) = 1/d$. Compute $G$, the minimum $1/G$, and compare with the true density $\frac{4}{15}$ of integers coprime to $30$.
2. Prove that $\sum_{e\le t}\mu^2(e)/\varphi(e) \ge \log t$ for $t \ge 1$.
3. Apply the Selberg sieve to $\{n \le x : n \equiv a \pmod q\}$ with $\gcd(a,q)=1$, using $g(d) = 1/d$ for $\gcd(d,q)=1$ (sieving only by primes not dividing $q$), and derive a bound of the form $\pi(x;q,a) \le (2+o(1))\,x/(\varphi(q)\log(x/q))$.
4. Explain why the Selberg sieve by itself cannot show that $\pi(x+y) - \pi(x) > 0$ for any $y$.

sources.ref: H. L. Montgomery & R. C. Vaughan, The large sieve, Mathematika 20 (1973)
